text: Small businesses in Egypt run on paper receipts. Every one of them ends up on an accountant's desk, typed in by hand. Qaid reads them first.
Small businesses are ninety percent of Egypt's private sector, and forty-three percent of its economy. Typing one receipt by hand takes three to five minutes, and one to three percent come out wrong.
So we built Qaid for the accounting office. The owner keeps their accountant. The accountant simply gets a lot more done.
This is the ledger: every client on one line. A red stamp means Qaid found something strange, like a price jump, a duplicate invoice, or a VAT spike.
A client opens a private link. No account, no app. They photograph a receipt, and the phone checks it for blur and glare before anything is sent.

Behind the scenes, two readers look at every receipt at the same time. One reads the layout, the other reads the image. A referee compares them field by field, and anything they disagree on is flagged, never quietly fixed.
Seconds later the entry appears on the board, next to the original receipt. Qaid has flagged a nine percent price rise. The accountant checks it, and confirms. Only confirmed entries ever count.
The accountant can also just ask. Every number in the answer comes from the records, never from a guess, and the answer streams in as it is written.
Missing a document? Qaid drafts the reminder in Arabic, ready to copy and send.
Month end is one click: Excel or PDF. And the whole app switches to Arabic, right to left.
On ten test receipts, every subtotal, VAT and total was right, in a median of six and a half seconds. They were clean renders, so real photos will do worse, and we say so.
Qaid prepares. The accountant decides. It is live now. Try it.
